I represent about a dozen artists, and when one of them gets a review, the first thing we both do is look for the adjectives. Not the long paragraphs, the small words in front of the adjectives. Fairly good is not good. Rather interesting is a polite way of saying not interesting enough. And quite is a trap, because quite good means only fairly good, while quite extraordinary means absolutely extraordinary. The review I fear most is not the bad one. A bad review at least means the critic cared. What really hurts an artist is the lukewarm review, the one that calls the work accomplished and thoughtful and then moves on. Nobody remembers it, and nobody goes to the show. When a critic writes absolutely or utterly, good or bad, they have made a decision, and that is the review people read.

The first serious review of my work called it derivative. I was thirty-one, and I read the word on a train and missed my stop. For about a year I told everybody the critic was utterly wrong. Then I went back to the show I had been accused of copying, and I had to admit he was partly right. My early pieces were heavy-handed. I explained everything, so nothing was left for the viewer. What I learned was not to make quieter work, but to trust the audience a little more. Twenty years later another critic called a big installation of mine overrated, and this time I simply asked myself one question. Did it fall flat because the idea was weak, or because the room was wrong? It was the room. That review made the next show better.
